ana-g16-a83.why: Transcalvarial herniation is displacement of swollen brain through a defect in the skull vault. At the foramen magnum, downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils is termed tonsillar herniation.

notes.A: The foramen magnum lies at the skull base. Downward movement of the cerebellar tonsils through it defines a different herniation pattern.

ana-g16-a84.why: The superior and inferior colliculi form the four elevations of the tectum on the posterior midbrain. The cerebral peduncles and intervening fossa are seen on the ventral surface.

notes.A: The cerebral peduncles form ventral prominences. The colliculi lie behind the cerebral aqueduct on the dorsal side.

ana-g16-a87.why: Brodmann area 4 in the precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. Area 6 includes premotor and supplementary motor areas, while area 8 includes the frontal eye field.

notes.A: Area 6 helps plan movement and area 8 includes gaze control. The chief primary cortical motor area is area 4.

ana-g16-a88.why: The pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus make up the classical Broca region. The posterior superior temporal cortex is traditionally associated with language comprehension.

notes.A: The superior temporal gyrus includes posterior auditory and language comprehension regions, while Broca’s region lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.

ana-g16-a89.why: Agraphaesthesia is failure to identify a figure traced on the skin despite sufficient primary sensory input. It usually points to impaired contralateral parietal processing of the spatial pattern.

notes.A: The parietal cortex combines tactile signals needed to recognise the traced figure, whereas frontal motor regions chiefly organise movement.

ana-g16-a90.why: Nasal retinal fibres from both eyes cross at the centre of the optic chiasm. They carry the temporal visual fields, so a central compressive lesion can produce bitemporal hemianopia.

notes.B: The crossing nasal fibres carry temporal field information from each eye, so central chiasmal compression can affect both temporal fields.

ana-g16-a121.why: Hippocampal fibres gather in the fimbria and continue into the paired crura. The crura join the body, which divides into columns projecting towards targets including the mammillary bodies.

notes.A: The body divides anteriorly into paired columns, with postcommissural fibres continuing towards the mammillary bodies.
notes.B: The crura converge beneath the corpus callosum to form the body of the fornix.
notes.C: The hippocampal commissure contains fibres passing between the two sides at the level of the crura.
notes.D: Each crus curves beneath the splenium as a continuation of the fimbria before joining the body.
notes.E: The fimbria forms where axons from the hippocampal surface collect along its medial edge.

ana-g16-c11.why: Oculomotor palsy weakens the muscle that elevates the upper eyelid and most extraocular muscles. A functioning lateral rectus and superior oblique then pull the eye outwards and usually downwards.

notes.A: Trochlear palsy weakens superior oblique and can cause vertical diplopia, while the upper lid elevator remains innervated.
notes.B: Abducent palsy weakens lateral rectus, so the affected eye has difficulty moving outwards and may rest medially.
notes.D: Loss of cervical sympathetic output causes mild ptosis and miosis, with the main extraocular motor nerves still working.
notes.E: The facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi. Its palsy impairs eyelid closure, with the upper lid elevator and extraocular muscles intact.

ana-g16-c12.why: The abducent nerve supplies the lateral rectus, which moves the eye laterally. The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique, and the oculomotor nerve supplies most of the other orbital muscles.

notes.A: The medial rectus adducts the eye and receives motor fibres from the oculomotor nerve.
notes.B: The superior rectus helps elevate the eye and is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes.C: The inferior rectus primarily depresses the eye and is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes.D: The levator raises the upper eyelid and receives motor fibres through the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.

ana-g16-c17.why: The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The tongue receives trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal and vagal sensory fibres, while hypoglossal and vagal pathways provide its motor supply.

notes.A: The lingual branch of the mandibular nerve carries touch, pain and temperature from most of the anterior tongue.
notes.B: Chorda tympani fibres of the facial nerve join the lingual nerve and carry taste from most of the anterior tongue.
notes.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior tongue and supplies the circumvallate papillae.
notes.D: The vagus carries sensation near the epiglottis and supplies palatoglossus through the pharyngeal plexus.

ana-g16-c18.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve ultimately activate the sphincter pupillae. Injury to these fibres can prevent constriction and leave the pupil dilated and poorly reactive.

notes.A: Optic nerve damage blocks afferent light signals from that eye. The pupil can still constrict when the other eye receives a stimulus.
notes.B: Interruption of cervical sympathetic fibres causes a small pupil because these fibres normally activate the pupillary dilator.
notes.C: The ophthalmic nerve mainly provides sensory input from the eye and forehead. It does not carry the preganglionic pupillary constrictor fibres.
notes.E: The facial nerve supplies eyelid closure through orbicularis oculi and carries secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland.

ana-g16-c20.why: After chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve, the combined nerve carries taste, oral sensation and salivary parasympathetic fibres. Sensory fibres from the lower teeth travel separately through the inferior alveolar nerve.

notes.A: Sublingual secretomotor fibres ultimately reach the gland from the submandibular ganglion by travelling with branches of the lingual nerve.
notes.C: Anterior tongue taste travels in chorda tympani fibres that temporarily run with the lingual nerve.
notes.D: Chorda tympani fibres reach the submandibular ganglion via the lingual nerve before postganglionic fibres supply the gland.
notes.E: The lingual nerve supplies the mucosa of the floor of the mouth as part of its general sensory distribution.

ana-g16-c21.why: The mylohyoid nerve leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before the latter enters the mandibular foramen. It travels down the mylohyoid groove to supply mylohyoid and the anterior digastric belly.

notes.A: The inferior alveolar nerve arises from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and gives off the mylohyoid branch.
notes.B: The mylohyoid groove runs below the mandibular foramen and carries the nerve towards the floor of the mouth.
notes.C: The anterior digastric belly receives the mylohyoid nerve, while the posterior belly receives a facial nerve branch.
notes.E: The submental artery supplies the region beneath mylohyoid and accompanies the nerve for part of its course.

ana-g16-c27.why: Firm eyelid closure tests orbicularis oculi, a facial expression muscle supplied by the facial nerve. Weakness lets an examiner open the eyelids more easily despite the patient's effort.

notes.B: Trigeminal motor fibres activate jaw muscles and mylohyoid. The trigeminal nerve provides sensory input to the corneal reflex.
notes.C: The abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus and moves the eye outwards without closing the lid.
notes.D: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique and helps depress the adducted eye without closing the lid.
notes.E: The superior division of the oculomotor nerve supplies the levator, which actively raises the upper lid.

ana-g16-c28.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends towards the larynx beside the trachea and oesophagus, commonly in their intervening groove. It reaches the larynx deep to the inferior constrictor.

notes.B: The recurrent nerve passes deep to the inferior constrictor. The thyrohyoid membrane is pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve.
notes.C: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus, looping around a vessel before ascending.
notes.D: The external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid. The recurrent nerve supplies the other intrinsic muscles.
notes.E: The combination is incorrect because the nerve enters deep to the inferior constrictor and arises from the vagus.

ana-g16-c30.why: Taste afferents from most of the anterior tongue pass in the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve. Their cell bodies lie in the geniculate ganglion before central processes reach the brainstem.

notes.A: The superior cervical ganglion contains sympathetic postganglionic neurons supplying structures in the head and neck.
notes.B: The trigeminal ganglion contains cell bodies for general sensation from the tongue through the lingual nerve.
notes.D: The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic relay for secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland.
notes.E: The submandibular ganglion contains parasympathetic neurons for salivary secretion, while sensory taste cell bodies lie in the geniculate ganglion.

ana-g16-c31.why: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves pass through the jugular foramen. Damage to the vagus there can weaken elevation of the palate by interrupting motor fibres to levator veli palatini.

notes.A: The lingual nerve carries pain signals from the anterior tongue and belongs to the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
notes.B: Tongue protrusion depends on genioglossus and the hypoglossal nerve, which passes through its own canal.
notes.C: Skin over the zygomatic prominence receives maxillary trigeminal branches that pass through the orbit and zygomatic bone.
notes.E: Right sternocleidomastoid helps rotate the face to the left. Turning the chin right relies mainly on the left muscle.

ana-g16-c33.why: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve leaves the skull through the foramen ovale. Stylohyoid instead receives a facial nerve branch after that nerve has left the stylomastoid foramen.

notes.A: Motor fibres from the mandibular nerve reach tensor tympani through a branch associated with the nerve to medial pterygoid.
notes.B: The mental branch of the inferior alveolar nerve carries sensation from the lower lip back to the mandibular division.
notes.C: The auriculotemporal nerve and other mandibular branches carry sensation from the temporomandibular joint.
notes.E: Inferior alveolar dental branches supply the lower premolars and carry information towards the mandibular division.

ana-g16-c34.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve gives lingual branches to the posterior third of the tongue and runs close to the tonsillar bed. Injury during removal of the tonsil can impair taste and general sensation there.

notes.B: Chorda tympani carries anterior tongue taste, while the lingual nerve provides general sensation in that region.
notes.C: The lingual nerve mainly supplies general sensation to the anterior tongue and floor of the mouth.
notes.D: The internal laryngeal branch of the vagus supplies the epiglottic region, farther posterior than the main glossopharyngeal territory.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles and does not carry the taste fibres described.

ana-g16-p36.why: The sciatic nerve forms from contributions of the anterior rami of lumbar and sacral spinal nerves, usually L4 to S3. Posterior rami supply the intrinsic back and its overlying skin.

notes.A: The sciatic nerve is the body's largest peripheral nerve and contains tibial and common fibular components.
notes.C: The sciatic nerve passes out of the pelvis into the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen.
notes.D: The usual sciatic course is beneath piriformis, although the components may follow variant courses around or through the muscle.
notes.E: The sciatic nerve is a major branch of the sacral plexus and carries much of its output to the lower limb.

ana-g16-p37.why: The pudendal nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis and above the sacrospinous ligament beside coccygeus. It curves around the ischial spine to reach the perineum through the lesser foramen.

notes.A: The pudendal nerve forms from anterior rami of the second through fourth sacral spinal nerves.
notes.B: The nerve runs with the internal pudendal vessels around the ischial spine and within the pudendal canal.
notes.C: The greater sciatic foramen is the nerve's exit from the pelvis, while the lesser foramen provides its route into the perineum.
notes.E: Pudendal branches carry sensation from much of the external genital region, although other nerves also supply parts of the skin.

ana-g16-p38.why: Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen into passages above and below the muscle. The superior gluteal nerve accompanies its vessels through the upper passage to supply gluteus medius and minimus.

notes.A: The sciatic nerve usually passes under piriformis into the deep gluteal region before descending towards the thigh.
notes.B: The pudendal nerve passes below piriformis and curves around the ischial spine before reaching the perineum.
notes.D: The lumbosacral trunk descends across the sacral ala to join the sacral plexus within the pelvis.
notes.E: The obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal to reach the medial compartment of the thigh.

ana-g16-n73.why: The supraorbital nerve is a terminal branch of the frontal nerve from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. It leaves the orbit at the supraorbital notch or foramen with accompanying vessels.

notes.A: The oculomotor nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure to supply most extraocular muscles.
notes.B: The infraorbital nerve is a maxillary division branch that emerges below the orbit through the infraorbital foramen.
notes.C: The supratrochlear nerve is a more medial branch of the frontal nerve that crosses the orbital rim separately.
notes.E: The notch carries an ophthalmic sensory branch. Neither the oculomotor nerve nor a branch of the maxillary division uses it.

ana-g16-k76.why: Adduction draws the thumb towards the plane of the palm. The main muscle producing this action is adductor pollicis, which is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

notes.A: The median nerve supplies several thenar muscles important for opposition and palmar abduction of the thumb.
notes.B: Radial nerve branches supply the long thumb extensors and abductor pollicis longus in the posterior forearm.
notes.C: The deep ulnar branch innervates adductor pollicis, which provides thumb adduction and contributes to a strong pinch.

ana-g16-k77.why: The ulnar nerve carries cutaneous sensation from the little finger, including its palmar surface. Sensory testing there helps distinguish an ulnar deficit from loss affecting principally the median nerve.

notes.A: The palmar thumb receives median nerve sensation, while much of its proximal dorsum receives superficial radial supply.
notes.B: The palmar tip of the little finger lies in the ulnar digital nerve territory with comparatively little overlap.
notes.C: Sensation at the palmar tip of the middle finger travels through a median digital branch.

ana-g16-k78.why: Loss of ulnar interosseous and medial lumbrical function leaves the long finger muscles relatively unbalanced. In a typical distal ulnar lesion the ring and little fingers can hyperextend at the knuckles and flex at the interphalangeal joints.

notes.A: Clawing is most marked in the ring and little fingers when their ulnar intrinsic muscles are paralysed.
notes.B: Wrist drop follows weakness of radial-innervated wrist extensors, especially with a radial nerve lesion proximal to their motor branches.
notes.C: Ape thumb posture reflects loss of median-innervated thenar function and impaired opposition rather than the usual ulnar pattern.

ana-g16-k79.why: Active flexion at the finger distal interphalangeal joints requires force transmission by flexor digitorum profundus. Flexion at the thumb interphalangeal joint likewise requires a functioning flexor pollicis longus muscle and tendon.

notes.A: Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the distal finger phalanges and bends the distal interphalangeal joints.
notes.B: Flexor pollicis longus inserts on the distal thumb phalanx and flexes its interphalangeal joint.
notes.C: Flexor carpi radialis acts at the wrist and attaches near the bases of the second and third metacarpals.

ana-g16-k81.why: Flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the middle phalanges and is the principal flexor of the proximal interphalangeal joints. Loss of isolated flexion at these joints can reflect injury to its tendons.

notes.A: Flexor carpi radialis attaches at the metacarpal bases and flexes the wrist rather than the finger joints.
notes.B: Each superficialis tendon splits around profundus and inserts on the middle phalanx, allowing it to bend the proximal interphalangeal joint.
notes.C: Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts through the pisiform complex and contributes to wrist flexion and ulnar deviation.

ana-g16-k89.why: During single-leg stance, the hip abductors of the supporting limb hold the opposite side of the pelvis level. Weakness of gluteus medius and minimus after superior gluteal nerve injury lets the unsupported side drop.

notes.A: The nerve to obturator internus supplies that muscle and superior gemellus, which principally rotate the hip laterally.
notes.B: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, whose abduction torque stabilises the pelvis during walking.
notes.C: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which is especially important for forceful hip extension.

ana-g16-k91.why: The femoral nerve arises from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It supplies quadriceps femoris, so interruption of its motor fibres weakens knee extension.

notes.A: L1 supplies other lumbar plexus branches, including the ilioinguinal nerve, but is outside the usual femoral root range.
notes.B: The second through fourth lumbar anterior rami contribute to the femoral nerve through their posterior divisions.
notes.C: L5 contributes to the lumbosacral trunk. The femoral nerve receives a more cranial contribution from L2.

ana-g16-k92.why: The femoral nerve gives direct cutaneous branches to the anterior thigh. Its long terminal sensory branch, the saphenous nerve, continues to supply skin along the medial leg and foot.

notes.A: The saphenous nerve carries sensation from the medial leg and medial foot as the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve.
notes.B: Anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve supply the skin over the front and medial side of the thigh.
notes.C: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises independently from the lumbar plexus and supplies anterolateral thigh skin.

ana-g16-k93.why: The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps in the anterior thigh and gives branches to iliacus in the pelvis. A lesion proximal to the relevant branches can weaken knee extension and reduce hip flexion.

notes.A: Quadratus lumborum receives segmental branches in the posterior abdominal wall and contributes to trunk side bending.
notes.B: Psoas muscles receive direct lumbar branches, while the femoral nerve supplies iliacus separately.
notes.C: Iliacus assists hip flexion, and the four quadriceps muscles extend the knee through the patella and its ligament.

ana-g16-k98.why: The inferior rectal nerve branches from the pudendal nerve and crosses the fat of the ischioanal fossa with its vessels. It supplies perianal skin and contributes motor fibres to the external anal sphincter.

notes.A: Direct sacral branches may supply parts of the pelvic floor or sphincter. The named nerve crossing the fat towards the anus is the inferior rectal nerve.
notes.B: The nerve to obturator internus follows the tendon region towards the muscle and supplies superior gemellus along its course.
notes.C: The inferior rectal nerve passes medially across the fossa from the pudendal canal towards the anal sphincter and skin.

ana-g16-b1.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior tongue uses a different combination of nerves, and most tongue movement depends on the hypoglossal nerve.

notes.A: The lingual nerve carries anterior general sensation, and chorda tympani carries taste from most of that region.
notes.B: Lingual branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve carry both sensory modalities from the posterior tongue.
notes.C: Protrusion depends on bilateral genioglossus activity, which is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

ana-g16-b2.why: In the posterior triangle, the spinal accessory nerve runs from sternocleidomastoid to trapezius. Weak elevation of the shoulder against resistance can reveal loss of trapezius function on the affected side.

notes.A: The right sternocleidomastoid rotates the head to the left. The left nerve has already supplied its sternocleidomastoid before reaching the triangle.
notes.B: Trapezius elevates the scapula during shoulder shrug and receives motor fibres from the ipsilateral accessory nerve.
notes.C: Cutaneous sensation over the triangle travels through cervical plexus branches. The accessory nerve chiefly provides motor output.

ana-g16-b3.why: The lingual nerve carries touch, pain and temperature from most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Chorda tympani fibres use part of the same route to carry taste.

notes.A: The lingual nerve arises from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and supplies the anterior oral mucosa.
notes.B: Chorda tympani carries anterior tongue taste and parasympathetic fibres for salivary glands rather than general tongue sensation.
notes.C: Vagal sensory fibres supply the tongue near the epiglottis, at the posterior end of its sensory territory.

ana-g16-b4.why: The abducens nerve supplies lateral rectus. When that muscle weakens, the eye cannot abduct normally and may turn medially under the relatively unopposed pull of medial rectus.

notes.A: Complete oculomotor palsy usually leaves the eye directed outwards and downwards, with possible ptosis and pupillary involvement.
notes.B: Trochlear palsy weakens superior oblique and usually produces vertical or torsional diplopia, especially on looking down.
notes.C: The right lateral rectus abducts the right eye, so a right abducens lesion can cause a convergent squint.

ana-g16-b5.why: A complete oculomotor lesion can disrupt parasympathetic constriction and weaken most extraocular muscles. The pupil becomes dilated, and lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye outwards and usually downwards.

notes.A: A small pupil suggests reduced sympathetic dilation, while a medial squint points towards weakness of lateral rectus.
notes.B: Loss of parasympathetic input can dilate the pupil, and preserved lateral rectus activity draws the eye laterally.
notes.C: A medial squint typically occurs when lateral rectus is weak, whereas the oculomotor lesion leaves lateral rectus innervated.

ana-g16-b8.why: Facial motor branches supply muscles of facial expression around the mouth, including the lower lip depressors. Taste over the posterior tongue and movement of the soft palate use different cranial pathways.

notes.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue and the circumvallate papillae.
notes.B: Most soft-palate muscles receive vagal motor fibres. Tensor veli palatini receives fibres from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
notes.C: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve supplies muscles that help depress and shape the lower lip.

ana-g16-t25.why: Cutaneous supply changes from supraclavicular branches over the upper chest to segmental thoracic and upper lumbar branches more inferiorly. Some lower segmental nerves send lateral branches over the iliac crest onto the buttock.

notes.A: Supraclavicular nerves descend across the clavicle from the cervical plexus and supply skin over the upper anterior chest.
notes.B: The fourth cervical dermatome extends over the clavicle and upper thoracic skin, with overlap at adjacent segmental boundaries.
notes.C: Anterior cutaneous branches reach the skin near the midline, with thoracic supply above and iliohypogastric supply near the pubis.
notes.D: Lateral cutaneous branches of the subcostal and iliohypogastric nerves cross the iliac crest to supply upper buttock skin.
notes.E: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the groin and adjacent upper medial thigh through its terminal cutaneous branches.

ana-gpq-15.why: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the intrinsic muscles that change tongue shape and most extrinsic muscles that reposition it. Palatoglossus receives vagal innervation through the pharyngeal plexus.

notes.A: Palatoglossus receives motor fibres from the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus and elevates the back of the tongue.
notes.B: The superior and inferior longitudinal muscles receive hypoglossal motor fibres and shorten or curl the tongue.
notes.C: Styloglossus receives hypoglossal fibres and pulls the tongue upwards and backwards from its styloid attachment.
notes.D: The vertical muscle receives hypoglossal fibres and flattens or broadens the tongue during contraction.
notes.E: Hyoglossus is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve and depresses the side of the tongue.

ana-gpq-42.why: Most pharyngeal arch muscle groups retain a characteristic cranial motor supply. The trigeminal, facial and glossopharyngeal nerves serve the first three arch groups, while vagal branches serve the fourth and sixth.

notes.A: The oculomotor nerve supplies extraocular muscles, which develop in a different mesodermal region from the pharyngeal arch muscles.
notes.B: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve supplies muscles of the first arch, including those used in mastication.
notes.C: The facial nerve supplies second-arch muscles, including the muscles of facial expression and the stapedius.
notes.D: Glossopharyngeal motor fibres supply stylopharyngeus, the principal muscle derivative of the third pharyngeal arch.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles formed chiefly from occipital somites, with palatoglossus supplied by the vagus.

ana-gpq-67.why: Cutaneous nerves to the upper limb may arise directly from the brachial plexus or as branches of its terminal nerves. The intercostobrachial nerve is an exception because it originates from a thoracic intercostal nerve.

notes.A: The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the radial nerve. The axillary nerve gives an upper lateral branch.
notes.B: The intercostobrachial nerve is usually the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve.
notes.C: The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm arises directly from the medial cord and supplies medial forearm skin.
notes.E: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm branches from the radial nerve rather than directly from the posterior cord.
notes.D: After supplying the anterior arm muscles, the musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

ana-gpq-68.why: The brachial plexus normally reorganises anterior rami of C5 through T1 into three trunks, each with anterior and posterior divisions. Their divisions then converge into cords named for their position around the axillary artery.

notes.B: The upper trunk forms from the fifth and sixth cervical roots, while the lowest pair forms the lower trunk.
notes.A: The seventh cervical anterior ramus continues as the middle trunk without uniting with a neighbouring root.
notes.C: The posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord behind the axillary artery.
notes.D: The anterior division of the lower trunk continues into the medial cord, carrying chiefly C8 and T1 fibres.
notes.E: The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks join to form the lateral cord.

ana-gpq-69.why: The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves branch from anterior rami before the trunks form. Their scapular targets differ from those of the nerves that arise farther along the plexus.

notes.A: The nerve to subclavius arises from the upper trunk and descends to the muscle beneath the clavicle.
notes.B: The dorsal scapular nerve usually arises from the fifth cervical root and supplies the rhomboids and part of levator scapulae.
notes.C: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and travels to latissimus dorsi.
notes.D: The long thoracic nerve usually receives fibres from the fifth through seventh cervical roots and supplies serratus anterior.

ana-gpq-70.why: Branches can leave the plexus before or after its trunks form. The suprascapular nerve leaves the upper trunk and runs towards the suprascapular notch to supply two scapular muscles.

notes.A: Supraclavicular nerves arise from the cervical plexus and supply skin over the clavicle, shoulder and upper chest.
notes.B: The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk and supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
notes.C: The long thoracic nerve collects contributions directly from cervical roots before descending on serratus anterior.
notes.D: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi on the posterior axillary wall.
notes.E: The intercostobrachial nerve is usually a lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve.

ana-gpq-71.why: Upper plexus injury affecting chiefly C5 and C6 weakens shoulder abduction and lateral rotation as well as elbow flexion and supination. The arm tends to rest adducted and internally rotated, with the forearm pronated.

notes.B: Weakness of supraspinatus and deltoid makes shoulder abduction difficult because both receive substantial upper plexus input.
notes.C: Wrist flexion can accompany the classical waiter's-tip posture, particularly when involvement extends to wrist extensors.
notes.D: Shoulder lateral rotators weaken, so the relatively unopposed internal rotators tend to turn the arm medially.
notes.E: Weak supination from biceps and supinator involvement allows the forearm to assume a pronated position.
notes.A: Facial expression depends on the facial nerve. An isolated upper brachial plexus injury affects the upper limb.

ana-gpq-72.why: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor and carries sensation over the upper lateral arm. Deltoid wasting and weak shoulder abduction therefore help localise dysfunction after a shoulder injury.

notes.C: Several muscles contribute to shoulder flexion, so preserved flexion alone does not establish axillary nerve damage.
notes.D: Extension also relies on muscles supplied by other nerves, so preserved extension is not a localising sign.
notes.E: The axillary cutaneous branch supplies the upper lateral arm. The lower lateral region receives a radial nerve branch.
notes.A: A sustained axillary motor lesion denervates deltoid and can flatten the normally rounded contour of the shoulder.
notes.B: Deltoid produces much of the force for shoulder abduction after supraspinatus initiates the movement.

ana-gpq-73.why: A radial nerve lesion at the humeral groove typically weakens wrist and finger extension and can impair dorsolateral hand sensation. Major triceps branches and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm often arise proximal to the lesion.

notes.A: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm usually arises before the radial nerve reaches the humeral groove.
notes.B: Most elbow extension is preserved if the triceps motor branches leave the nerve above the lesion.
notes.C: The superficial radial sensory branch supplies part of the dorsolateral hand, with the first dorsal web space a useful landmark.
notes.D: Loss of radial motor supply to the wrist extensors allows unopposed flexion, producing wrist drop.
notes.E: Shoulder rotation depends on muscles around the glenohumeral joint and is not fixed by a radial lesion in the arm.

ana-gpq-75.why: The recurrent median branch supplies most thenar muscles, and median digital branches supply the lateral two lumbricals. The deep ulnar branch supplies adductor pollicis and the medial two lumbricals.

notes.A: Adductor pollicis receives motor fibres from the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and contributes to pinch.
notes.B: The medial two lumbricals receive ulnar motor supply, while the lateral pair receive median supply.
notes.C: The superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis is usually supplied by the recurrent median branch.
notes.D: Abductor pollicis brevis receives recurrent median fibres and moves the thumb away from the plane of the palm.
notes.E: Opponens pollicis receives median motor fibres and rotates the first metacarpal during thumb opposition.

ana-gpq-82.why: Below the inguinal ligament the femoral nerve lies on iliacus lateral to the femoral artery and outside its sheath. The artery lies near the surface landmark halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis.

notes.A: The nerve lies lateral to the vessels, but the femoral sheath encloses the vessels and femoral canal.
notes.C: The sheath's lateral compartment contains the femoral artery. The femoral nerve lies farther laterally outside the sheath.
notes.B: The artery is medial to the femoral nerve and lateral to the femoral vein at the upper thigh.
notes.D: The midinguinal point is halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis and marks the artery.
notes.E: The femoral nerve is accessible below the ligament, where clinicians can identify it lateral to the artery for regional anaesthesia.

ana-gpq-84.why: The femoral nerve forms in the lumbar plexus from posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It descends into the thigh between psoas major and iliacus.

notes.A: Posterior rami supply the back and do not form the lumbar plexus, which is derived from anterior rami.
notes.B: The anterior ramus of L2 is the uppermost usual contribution to the femoral nerve.
notes.C: The anterior ramus of L3 contributes fibres to the femoral nerve through its posterior division.
notes.D: The anterior ramus of L4 provides the lowest usual root contribution to the femoral nerve.
notes.E: The anterior ramus of L5 contributes to the lumbosacral trunk rather than the femoral nerve.

ana-gpq-85.why: Femoral nerve branches supply anterior thigh muscles and transmit sensation from the anterior thigh and medial leg. Several nearby muscles and cutaneous territories receive separate lumbar plexus branches.

notes.A: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises directly from the lumbar plexus as a separate nerve.
notes.D: Adductor brevis normally receives motor fibres from the obturator nerve in the medial thigh.
notes.E: Gracilis receives obturator motor supply and contributes to hip adduction and knee flexion.
notes.B: The nerve to pectineus usually branches from the femoral nerve near the inguinal ligament.
notes.C: The saphenous nerve is the femoral nerve's long sensory branch to the medial leg and foot.

ana-gpq-87.why: The obturator nerve arises from the lumbar plexus and reaches the medial thigh through the obturator canal. It supplies several adductors and gives articular branches as well as a variable cutaneous branch.

notes.A: The obturator nerve forms from anterior divisions of lumbar anterior rami, usually L2 to L4.
notes.C: Its pelvic exit is the obturator canal. The passage beneath piriformis transmits branches of the sacral plexus.
notes.D: A cutaneous branch can supply a small patch of skin on the medial thigh, although the area is variable.
notes.B: Obturator motor branches supply most muscles in the medial compartment, including adductor longus and gracilis.
notes.E: The obturator nerve gives articular branches to the hip and can contribute sensory supply to the knee.

ana-gpq-88.why: Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen into two passages. Several sacral plexus branches and the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal vessels travel through the lower passage towards the buttock or perineum.

notes.A: The inferior gluteal nerve and vessels pass below piriformis to reach the deep surface of gluteus maximus.
notes.B: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh leaves beneath piriformis and carries sensation from the posterior thigh.
notes.C: The pudendal nerve exits below piriformis before turning around the ischial spine into the perineum.
notes.D: The internal pudendal artery leaves alongside the pudendal nerve and returns through the lesser sciatic foramen.
notes.E: The nerve to obturator internus leaves through the lower passage and then reaches its muscle by the lesser foramen.

ana-gpq-90.why: The sciatic nerve carries lumbar and sacral fibres into the posterior thigh. Its tibial component supplies most hamstrings and continues towards the popliteal fossa, where the tibial nerve lies superficial to the central vessels.

notes.A: The sciatic nerve gathers contributions from L4 through S3 in the sacral plexus.
notes.B: It gives muscular branches in the thigh. Skin over the posterior thigh is supplied chiefly by a separate cutaneous nerve.
notes.C: The tibial division supplies the hamstring part of adductor magnus, which contributes to hip extension.
notes.D: In the central popliteal bundle the tibial nerve lies closest to the surface, with the popliteal vein and artery deeper.

ana-gpq-97.why: Dermatomes map skin to spinal segments, with neighbouring territories overlapping. The thumb, upper medial arm, umbilicus and inguinal region are useful approximate landmarks for common segmental maps.

notes.A: The first cervical nerve usually lacks a distinct cutaneous dermatome. Other cervical and trigeminal nerves supply these regions.
notes.B: The sixth cervical dermatome commonly includes the thumb and lateral forearm, although its borders overlap adjacent segments.
notes.C: The umbilicus is the standard surface landmark for the tenth thoracic dermatome.
notes.D: The second thoracic dermatome includes the upper medial arm, supplied in part through the intercostobrachial nerve.
notes.E: The first lumbar dermatome reaches the groin near the inguinal ligament.

ana-gpq-99.why: Reflexes help localise dysfunction to the spinal segments and peripheral nerves that form their arcs. Tendon responses test stretch pathways, while stroking the abdominal skin elicits a superficial cutaneous response.

notes.D: The ankle reflex is mediated primarily by S1 through the tibial nerve to the plantarflexors.
notes.A: The biceps tendon reflex tests the musculocutaneous pathway, mainly through the fifth and sixth cervical segments.
notes.B: The radial nerve carries the triceps reflex, whose dominant segment is C7 with contribution commonly assigned to C8.
notes.C: The patellar tendon reflex tests mainly the third and fourth lumbar segments through the femoral nerve.
notes.E: The superficial abdominal responses use thoracic segments, with upper and lower quadrants involving different levels.

ana-gpq-112.why: General sensation and taste follow different routes in the anterior tongue. Fungiform taste fibres travel with chorda tympani, whereas circumvallate papillae receive glossopharyngeal fibres despite lying near the anterior side of the terminal sulcus.

notes.A: Filiform papillae lack taste buds, but the lingual nerve carries general sensory information from their region.
notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the circumvallate papillae near the terminal sulcus.
notes.C: Taste from fungiform papillae reaches the facial nerve through its chorda tympani branch.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles, while taste from fungiform papillae uses facial sensory fibres.
notes.D: Glossopharyngeal taste fibres supply the large vallate papillae just anterior to the terminal sulcus.

ana-gpq-115.why: Branches of the maxillary and mandibular divisions of the trigeminal nerve convey most general sensation from the palate, teeth and oral mucosa. The facial buccal branch instead supplies muscles around the cheek.

notes.E: The facial buccal branch supplies muscles including buccinator. Cheek mucosal sensation travels mainly through the trigeminal buccal nerve.
notes.A: The greater palatine nerve supplies much of the hard palate and adjacent palatal gingiva.
notes.B: The nasopalatine nerve reaches the anterior hard palate through the incisive canal and supplies its mucosa.
notes.C: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth, with terminal branches reaching the chin and lower lip.
notes.D: Superior alveolar branches supply the maxillary teeth and related gingival tissues.

ana-osa-41.why: The trigeminal nerve carries the main general somatic afferent supply of the face, oral and nasal cavities and parts of the dura. These fibres convey modalities including touch, pain and temperature.

notes.A: The olfactory nerve carries smell from the olfactory epithelium as a specialised sensory modality.
notes.B: The oculomotor nerve supplies most orbital muscles and carries parasympathetic fibres to the ciliary ganglion.
notes.C: The trochlear nerve carries motor fibres to superior oblique, which contributes to eye depression and intorsion.
notes.E: The abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus, the muscle that moves the eye laterally.

ana-osa-42.why: Branchial motor fibres of the facial nerve supply muscles derived mainly from the second pharyngeal arch. These include the muscles of facial expression, stapedius and the posterior belly of digastric.

notes.A: The optic nerve carries visual sensory information from the retina to central visual pathways.
notes.B: The oculomotor nerve supplies orbital muscles and carries parasympathetic fibres, using somatic and visceral motor components.
notes.C: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, an extraocular muscle receiving somatic motor fibres.
notes.D: The abducent nerve activates lateral rectus through somatic motor fibres rather than an arch-derived motor pathway.

ana-osa-46.why: The oculomotor nerve controls the upper eyelid elevator and most extraocular muscles. Loss of that control can cause ptosis and misalignment, while forward displacement of the globe generally points to an orbital process.

notes.A: A complete lesion weakens medial rectus, allowing relatively unopposed lateral rectus to turn the eye outwards.
notes.B: Ptosis occurs because levator palpebrae superioris loses its oculomotor motor supply.
notes.C: Asymmetrical weakness can misalign the eyes, producing diplopia when both eyes are open.
notes.D: The lesion can weaken adduction, elevation and depression because several extraocular muscles share oculomotor supply.

ana-osa-47.why: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, which helps depress the adducted eye and intort it. Weakness commonly causes vertical diplopia during tasks such as reading or going downstairs.

notes.A: Near focusing depends partly on the ciliary muscle and its oculomotor parasympathetic supply, rather than the trochlear nerve.
notes.B: Abduction depends on lateral rectus, which receives motor fibres from the abducent nerve.
notes.D: Superior rectus and inferior oblique contribute to upward gaze and receive oculomotor motor supply.
notes.E: A fixed dilated pupil can follow loss of oculomotor parasympathetic input to the sphincter of the pupil.

ana-osa-49.why: Chorda tympani leaves the facial nerve within the temporal bone before the main trunk enters the parotid gland. A lesion confined to the parotid segment therefore typically weakens facial expression while preserving anterior tongue taste.

notes.A: Facial fibres loop near the abducens nucleus in the pons, so a lesion there can affect lateral gaze and facial movement together.
notes.B: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves share the internal acoustic meatus, where one lesion can affect both.
notes.D: A lesion upstream of the nerve to stapedius can cause hyperacusis by interrupting damping of ossicular motion.
notes.E: Bilateral cortical input usually preserves forehead movement after a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion, while the opposite lower face is weak.

ana-osa-50.why: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance information. Its dysfunction can affect sound perception and vestibular responses, whereas Bell's palsy is an acute peripheral facial motor palsy without an identified cause.

notes.A: Asymmetric vestibular activity can cause vertigo, an illusory sense of movement.
notes.C: A vestibular imbalance can produce nystagmus through asymmetric input to the pathways controlling gaze.
notes.D: Cochlear or cochlear nerve dysfunction can produce tinnitus, the perception of sound without an external source.
notes.E: Damage to the cochlear division can impair sound transmission to the brain and cause sensorineural hearing loss.

ana-osa-b11.why: The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve enters the middle ear and contributes to the tympanic plexus on the promontory. This plexus provides sensation to the mucosa of the cavity.

notes.A: The facial nerve passes through its bony canal and gives motor fibres to stapedius. The tympanic plexus supplies the cavity mucosa.
notes.B: The auriculotemporal branch of the trigeminal nerve supplies part of the external ear and outer surface of the tympanic membrane.
notes.D: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance signals from receptors in the inner ear.
notes.E: The auricular branch of the vagus supplies parts of the external acoustic canal rather than the middle ear mucosa.

ana-g16-a1.why: The distal median nerve can lose its anterior interosseous branch to pronator quadratus. Branches to pronator teres usually leave earlier, so pronation weakens but remains possible.

notes.B: Pronator teres can still work, but loss of anterior interosseous supply weakens pronator quadratus and reduces overall pronation.

ana-g16-a2.why: There are eight pairs of cervical spinal nerves even though there are seven cervical vertebrae. Each spinal nerve divides into an anterior and a posterior ramus, yielding eight anterior rami on each side.

notes.B: The eighth cervical nerve emerges between the seventh cervical and first thoracic vertebrae and also has an anterior ramus.

ana-g16-a7.why: The radial nerve supplies triceps in the posterior arm before traversing the lateral intermuscular septum. A distal lesion at the septum chiefly threatens motor branches to muscles in the forearm.

notes.A: Triceps receives branches proximal to the septum, so its motor supply is usually preserved after a lesion at that level.

ana-g16-a8.why: The interossei and medial two lumbricals contribute strongly to flexion at the knuckles of the ring and little fingers. Their motor supply comes from the ulnar nerve, so they are spared by an isolated median lesion.

notes.A: Median injury can weaken long finger flexion, but the ulnar nerve supplies the intrinsic flexors of the ring and little finger knuckles.

ana-g16-a9.why: The suprascapular nerve supplies infraspinatus, which creates lateral rotation at the shoulder. Injury can weaken that action while the axillary nerve still supplies teres minor, another lateral rotator.

notes.B: Infraspinatus receives suprascapular motor fibres and contributes to externally rotating the humerus in the glenoid cavity.

ana-g16-a14.why: The dorsal scapular nerve usually leaves the anterior ramus of C5 before it joins C6 to form the upper trunk. Its principal targets are the rhomboids and part of levator scapulae.

notes.A: The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius, whereas the dorsal scapular nerve generally arises more proximally.

ana-g16-a16.why: The obturator nerve reaches the medial thigh through the obturator canal and supplies most adductors. The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstring muscles of the posterior thigh, mainly through its tibial division.

notes.A: Obturator branches supply medial thigh adductors, including adductor longus and gracilis, while sciatic branches supply the hamstrings.

ana-g16-a18.why: The adductor canal carries the femoral vessels and saphenous nerve deep to sartorius. The main obturator nerve divides after reaching the medial thigh and distributes branches around adductor brevis.

notes.A: The main obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal and divides into branches around adductor brevis.

ana-g16-a21.why: The femoral nerve forms from posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It reaches the thigh lateral to the femoral vessels after passing under the inguinal ligament.

notes.B: The femoral nerve receives fibres from the second, third and fourth lumbar anterior rami in the usual pattern.

ana-g16-a27.why: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh carries sensation from the anterolateral skin. Vastus lateralis is a quadriceps muscle in the anterior compartment and receives motor fibres from the femoral nerve.

notes.A: Vastus lateralis receives motor supply through a branch of the femoral nerve and contributes to extension of the knee.

ana-g16-a28.why: The saphenous nerve is a cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve. It becomes superficial near the medial knee, then supplies skin along the medial leg and part of the medial foot.

notes.B: Femoral sensory fibres reach below the knee in the saphenous branch even though its main motor branches supply the thigh.

ana-g16-a35.why: Cutaneous branches from thoracic spinal segments supply the anterior chest and abdomen, with L1 contributing near the groin and pubis. Sacral segments chiefly serve regions of the lower limb and perineum.

notes.A: The lower anterior abdomen receives lumbar as well as lower thoracic branches. Sacral dermatomes do not continue the anterior trunk series to the pubis.

ana-g16-a41.why: Intercostal nerves give named lateral and anterior cutaneous branches that reach the skin. Their collateral branches travel with small vessels along the border of the lower rib within the intercostal space.

notes.A: The lateral cutaneous branches supply skin on the side of the chest, while anterior cutaneous branches emerge near the sternum.

ana-g16-a73.why: The first cervical nerve chiefly supplies muscle and usually has no distinct cutaneous dermatome. Skin over the neck and scalp is supplied by other upper cervical branches, including branches from the second cervical nerve.

notes.B: The dorsal ramus of the first cervical nerve is the suboccipital nerve, which primarily supplies the deep suboccipital muscles.

ana-g16-a74.why: The greater occipital nerve arises from the medial branch of the second cervical posterior ramus. It ascends to supply posterior scalp, while the lesser occipital nerve comes from the cervical plexus.

notes.A: The cervical plexus uses anterior rami and gives the lesser occipital nerve. The greater occipital nerve comes from the posterior ramus of C2.

ana-g16-a85.why: The abducent nerve crosses the venous compartment of the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery. The oculomotor, trochlear and upper trigeminal divisions instead run in the lateral wall.

notes.B: Unlike the nerves embedded in the lateral wall, the abducent nerve runs with the artery within the sinus proper.

ana-g16-p57.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from sacral levels S2 to S4 to pelvic and distal bowel plexuses. They also provide a route for visceral afferents.

notes.A: Somatic afferents from pelvic floor skin or skeletal muscle chiefly run in somatic nerves, such as the pudendal nerve.
notes.B: Sympathetic fibres reach the pelvic plexus through hypogastric pathways and sacral splanchnic nerves, which are a separate group.
notes.D: Special visceral efferent fibres supply pharyngeal arch muscles through cranial nerves, rather than pelvic smooth muscle or glands.
notes.E: Special somatic afferent pathways carry visual, auditory or vestibular information through cranial nerves.

ana-g16-p58.why: Parasympathetic activity promotes relaxation of smooth muscle and increased blood flow within genital erectile tissues. Filling of the vascular spaces produces engorgement of the vestibular bulbs and clitoral tissue.

notes.A: Genital arousal is associated with increased vaginal lubrication, including fluid movement across the vaginal wall.
notes.C: The greater vestibular glands secrete mucus. The adjacent vestibular bulbs contain the erectile tissue that engorges.
notes.D: Increased blood filling generally enlarges erectile tissue in the clitoris during arousal.
notes.E: Flaccidity follows reduced blood filling and detumescence, whereas the parasympathetic response promotes engorgement.

ana-g16-n74.why: Edinger–Westphal preganglionic fibres travel with the oculomotor nerve and synapse in the ciliary ganglion. Their targets promote pupillary constriction and accommodation, while the dilator pupillae receives sympathetic supply.

notes.A: The greater petrosal nerve carries facial preganglionic fibres from the superior salivatory region towards the lacrimal pathway.
notes.B: Superior salivatory fibres enter chorda tympani and travel with the lingual nerve to supply the submandibular gland after a ganglionic relay.
notes.C: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion before reaching the gland on trigeminal branches.
notes.D: Parasympathetic fibres from the inferior salivatory nucleus reach the otic ganglion before supplying the parotid.

ana-g16-b14.why: The deep petrosal nerve carries sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus. It joins the greater petrosal nerve to form a mixed autonomic pathway through the pterygoid canal.

notes.A: The nerve of the pterygoid canal includes sympathetic fibres contributed by the deep petrosal nerve and parasympathetic fibres from the greater petrosal nerve.
notes.C: The lesser petrosal nerve principally conveys glossopharyngeal preganglionic parasympathetic fibres towards the otic ganglion to supply the parotid.
notes.B: The deep petrosal nerve carries postganglionic sympathetic fibres that have already relayed in the superior cervical ganglion.

ana-g16-b15.why: The vagus supplies parasympathetic fibres to thoracic organs and much of the abdominal digestive tract. The distal hindgut and pelvic organs instead receive parasympathetic fibres from sacral outflow.

notes.C: Glossopharyngeal parasympathetic fibres relay in the otic ganglion to supply the parotid gland.
notes.A: Sacral spinal outflow gives pelvic parasympathetic fibres, while the named thoracic and upper abdominal organs mainly use the vagus.
notes.B: Vagal branches reach the heart and lungs, while oesophageal vagal pathways descend to upper abdominal organs.

ana-g16-b16.why: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. They then use branches of the maxillary nerve and a communicating branch to reach the lacrimal nerve, which conveys them to the gland.

notes.A: The zygomatic nerve carries postganglionic fibres into the orbit after receiving them in the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.B: A communication from the zygomaticotemporal branch transfers these fibres to the lacrimal nerve in the conventional pathway.
notes.C: The lacrimal nerve carries the postganglionic secretomotor fibres on the final segment of their route to the gland.

ana-osa-b19.why: The submandibular gland receives postganglionic fibres from the submandibular ganglion after facial preganglionic fibres travel through chorda tympani. The pterygopalatine ganglion instead relays fibres reaching lacrimal, nasal, palatal and pharyngeal targets.

notes.A: Postganglionic fibres reach the lacrimal gland via zygomatic and lacrimal branches after relaying in the pterygopalatine ganglion.
notes.B: Posterior nasal branches carry secretomotor fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion to glands in the nasal mucosa.
notes.C: Branches of the palatine nerves carry postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion to glands in the palate.
notes.D: The pharyngeal branch carries postganglionic fibres towards glands in the mucosa of the nasopharynx.

ana-osa-b20.why: Inferior salivatory preganglionic fibres leave in the glossopharyngeal nerve and continue through the tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve. They synapse in the otic ganglion, whose output reaches the parotid gland.

notes.A: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres originate in the superior salivatory region and relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion.
notes.B: Chorda tympani carries facial parasympathetic fibres that relay in the submandibular ganglion and supply the submandibular gland.
notes.C: The sublingual gland receives facial parasympathetic input through chorda tympani with a submandibular ganglion relay.
notes.D: Minor lingual glands have regional parasympathetic pathways. The classical inferior salivatory and otic ganglion pathway supplies the parotid.

ana-gpq-165.why: The right adrenal gland is usually pyramidal and relates to the liver and inferior vena cava. The crescent-shaped left gland lies behind the upper stomach and partly relates to the lesser sac.

notes.E: The stomach lies on the left, and the left suprarenal gland helps form its posterior bed.
notes.A: The right gland has a roughly pyramidal shape and caps the upper part of the right kidney.
notes.B: Renal fascia and fat surround the gland, and its posterior relation includes the diaphragm and intervening fascial tissue.
notes.C: The left gland is usually crescent shaped and extends down the upper medial side of the left kidney.
notes.D: Part of the left gland lies posterior to the peritoneal lining of the lesser sac in the stomach bed.

ana-g16-c4.why: The tympanic membrane lies between the external acoustic canal and the air-filled tympanic cavity. It forms most of the lateral wall of the middle ear and transmits sound vibrations to the malleus.

notes.A: The inner ear contains the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth, which lie deeper than the external canal and tympanic cavity.
notes.C: The medial wall of the middle ear faces the labyrinth and contains the promontory and the oval and round windows.
notes.D: The membrane vibrates in response to sound pressure and transfers motion to the ossicular chain.
notes.E: Otoscopy allows the membrane to be examined at the medial end of the external acoustic canal.

ana-g16-c5.why: The tegmen tympani is a thin plate of the temporal bone forming the roof of the tympanic cavity. It separates the middle ear from the dura and structures of the middle cranial fossa above.

notes.A: Tensor tympani is a muscle inserted on the malleus. Its canal lies below an anterior part of the bony roof.
notes.B: The separating layer is compact temporal bone. A fibrous fascial sheet does not form this cranial partition.
notes.D: A tympanic fascial label describes soft tissue rather than the defined temporal bone plate over the cavity.
notes.E: A border is a margin. The tegmen is the plate that spans the cavity and forms its roof.

ana-g16-c6.why: The organ of Corti rests on the basilar membrane of the cochlear duct. Deflection of its hair cells during cochlear vibration converts mechanical energy into signals that are conveyed by the cochlear nerve.

notes.A: The anterior semicircular canal contains a duct whose ampulla senses angular acceleration in its plane.
notes.B: The lateral duct contains a receptor in its ampulla that signals rotation in a nearly horizontal plane.
notes.D: The utricle detects linear acceleration and head tilt through a macula oriented chiefly in the horizontal plane.
notes.E: The saccular macula detects linear acceleration and is oriented chiefly in a vertical plane.

ana-g16-c7.why: The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle in the orbit. The other listed pathways supply parts of the external or middle ear through sensory branches or through the facial motor branch to stapedius.

notes.A: The auriculotemporal nerve supplies parts of the auricle, external acoustic canal and lateral surface of the tympanic membrane.
notes.B: The facial nerve supplies stapedius, a small muscle that acts on the stapes within the middle ear.
notes.C: The auricular branch of the vagus supplies sensory fibres to part of the external acoustic canal and auricle.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal tympanic branch supplies middle ear mucosa through the tympanic plexus.

ana-g16-c38.why: Endolymph fills the cochlear duct and the other compartments of the membranous labyrinth. It is rich in potassium compared with the perilymph that surrounds the membranous structures within the bony labyrinth.

notes.A: Perilymph is outside the membranous labyrinth and occupies the scala vestibuli and scala tympani in the cochlea.
notes.B: Cerebrospinal fluid occupies spaces around the central nervous system, while the membranous labyrinth contains its own inner fluid.
notes.D: The inner-ear fluid has a specialised ionic composition, maintained in the cochlear duct by processes including potassium secretion.
notes.E: Aqueous humour circulates in the anterior segment of the eye, where it contributes to intraocular pressure.

ana-g16-c39.why: The facial nerve gives a motor branch to stapedius, and chorda tympani crosses the tympanic cavity. The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the middle ear mucosa through its tympanic branch and plexus.

notes.A: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique and the cochlear division carries signals from the inner ear.
notes.B: The vestibulocochlear nerve serves inner-ear receptors, while the abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus in the orbit.
notes.D: The nasociliary nerve provides orbital and nasal sensation, while the trochlear nerve supplies an extraocular muscle.
notes.E: Facial branches reach the middle ear, but the optic nerve carries visual signals from the retina.

ana-g16-c40.why: The pharyngotympanic tube extends from the anterior wall of the middle ear to the lateral nasopharynx. Its opening allows ventilation and helps balance pressure across the tympanic membrane.

notes.A: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears into the inferior nasal meatus from the lacrimal sac.
notes.C: The uterine tube connects the uterine cavity to a fimbrial opening near the ovary and belongs to the reproductive tract.
notes.D: The palatoglossal fold is a boundary of the opening from the oral cavity to the oropharynx.
notes.E: The nasolabial fold is a surface crease between the cheek and lip, lateral to the nose.

ana-g16-c41.why: Tensor tympani pulls on the malleus and receives mandibular trigeminal motor fibres. Stapedius acts on the stapes and receives facial motor fibres, providing a second way to regulate ossicular movement.

notes.A: Stapedius belongs to the middle ear, while tensor veli palatini tenses the soft palate and helps open the auditory tube.
notes.B: Tensor palati refers to the soft-palate tensor. The tensor attached to the malleus is tensor tympani.
notes.C: The specific tympanic tensor is the muscle attached to the malleus. “Tympanic muscle” alone does not name the pair precisely.
notes.E: Levator veli palatini raises the soft palate during swallowing. Stapedius acts on an ossicle inside the tympanic cavity.

ana-g16-b17.why: The cochlear division carries hearing signals, while the vestibular division carries information about head motion and orientation. Damage can therefore cause hearing symptoms or disturb gaze and balance, depending on the fibres involved.

notes.A: Cochlear nerve dysfunction can reduce sensorineural hearing and may produce tinnitus on the affected side.
notes.B: Unequal vestibular input can drive involuntary rhythmic eye movement through the gaze-stabilising reflex pathways.
notes.C: A sudden imbalance in vestibular signals can create an apparent sensation that the person or surroundings are moving.

ana-gpq-17.why: The oral tongue has several types of papillae. Filiform papillae provide a widespread mechanical surface, while fungiform and vallate papillae contribute to taste and occur in distinct patterns.

notes.B: Filiform papillae cover much of the presulcal dorsum. Fungiform papillae are more characteristic of the tip and margins.
notes.E: The vallate region near the sulcus has many taste buds along the walls of its trenches, while each fungiform papilla near the tip usually has few.
notes.A: Vallate papillae form a row on the anterior side of the V-shaped terminal sulcus.
notes.C: Filiform papillae provide friction mechanically and do not contain taste buds in the normal tongue.
notes.D: Fungiform papillae have rounded tops and can carry taste buds, often on their upper surface.

ana-gpq-19.why: The anterior tongue mucosa develops chiefly from first-arch lateral swellings. The posterior mucosa develops mainly from the hypobranchial eminence, whereas most tongue muscles are formed by migrating occipital myotomes.

notes.C: The tuberculum impar is a median first-arch swelling associated with the anterior tongue. The posterior third forms from the hypobranchial eminence.
notes.D: Later arch tissue overgrows the second-arch swelling, leaving no substantial second-arch territory in the adult tongue mucosa.
notes.A: Occipital myotomes contribute most tongue muscles and are accompanied by the hypoglossal nerve during development.
notes.B: Paired first-arch lateral lingual swellings enlarge and merge to form most of the mucosa of the oral tongue.
notes.E: The caudal fourth-arch region contributes mucosa near the epiglottis, where vagal sensory supply is retained.

ana-gpq-109.why: The terminal sulcus marks the boundary between oral and pharyngeal tongue. Most oral papillae lie in front of it, including the vallate row, while the valleculae lie between the tongue base and epiglottis.

notes.D: Vallate papillae form a row just anterior to the sulcus even though they receive glossopharyngeal innervation.
notes.E: A vallecula is a mucosal recess between the pharyngeal tongue and epiglottis, behind the terminal sulcus.
notes.A: Filiform papillae cover much of the anterior dorsum and provide a textured surface for moving food.
notes.B: The terminal sulcus forms the V-shaped posterior boundary of the oral part of the tongue.
notes.C: Minor lingual glands are present anteriorly, including mixed glands on the underside near the tip.

ana-gpq-110.why: Taste buds occur in fungiform, vallate and foliate papillae, where their sensory cells contact afferent fibres. The numerous keratinised filiform papillae instead help the tongue grip and move food.

notes.A: Filiform papillae are slender mechanical structures that increase friction and lack the sensory cells of taste buds.
notes.B: Fungiform papillae are scattered on the anterior tongue and can contain taste buds on their exposed surfaces.
notes.C: Vallate papillae contain taste buds chiefly along their lateral walls facing the surrounding trenches.
notes.D: The posterolateral foliate folds can contain taste buds within the epithelium of the grooves.

ana-osa-b2.why: The external acoustic canal has a lateral cartilaginous third followed by a medial bony two-thirds. Hairs and ceruminous glands are features of the thicker skin of the outer segment.

notes.A: Cartilage supports the lateral canal, while the temporal bone forms the deeper portion nearest the tympanic membrane.
notes.B: The lateral cartilaginous portion has thicker skin with hair follicles that help trap debris.
notes.C: The medial bony portion has thin skin closely applied to bone and normally lacks hair follicles.
notes.D: Ceruminous glands lie in the outer cartilaginous skin and contribute secretions that form earwax.

ana-sa-e-47.why: The terms identify surface regions from proximal limb landmarks to the lower leg. Axillary denotes the armpit, coxal the hip, femoral the thigh, acromial the shoulder tip and crural the leg below the knee.

notes.B: The thigh is femoral and the shoulder tip is acromial, so neither matches the first two regions named.
notes.C: The shoulder tip is acromial, whereas the first region is the axilla under the shoulder joint.
notes.D: The crural region is the leg between knee and ankle, which is the last region in the sequence.
notes.E: Coxal correctly refers to the hip, but the sequence begins with the axilla and ends with the leg.

ana-g16-k94.why: The transpyloric plane is conventionally drawn at about the first lumbar vertebra. It helps describe the positions of upper abdominal structures, though the pylorus and other organs shift with posture and filling.

notes.A: Addison’s transpyloric plane usually crosses the body or lower border of the first lumbar vertebra.
notes.B: The subcostal plane passes through the inferior points of the costal margins and lies near the third lumbar vertebra.
notes.C: The transumbilical plane passes through the umbilicus, which usually overlies a lower and more variable lumbar level.

ana-g16-k95.why: Addison’s plane is located on the anterior body surface halfway from the jugular notch to the upper border of the pubic symphysis. It corresponds approximately to the first lumbar vertebra.

notes.A: The lower points of the costal margins define the subcostal plane, which typically lies near the third lumbar vertebra.
notes.B: A line joining the highest iliac crests lies near the fourth lumbar spinous level or the interval below it.
notes.C: The midpoint between these two midline landmarks defines the surface level of the transpyloric plane.

ana-g16-k96.why: Addison’s transpyloric plane lies near the first lumbar vertebra. Classically it meets the ninth costal cartilages and approximates the gallbladder fundus and superior mesenteric artery origin, with individual variation.

notes.B: The fundus commonly projects near the right ninth costal cartilage where the lateral rectus border meets the costal margin.
notes.A: The tips of the ninth costal cartilages are the anterior costal landmarks for this horizontal plane.
notes.C: The superior mesenteric artery originates from the front of the abdominal aorta near the first lumbar level.

ana-g16-t26.why: The lower thoracic cage overlaps upper abdominal organs. The diaphragm separates several of them from the chest, while posterior lower ribs also overlie the upper parts of the retroperitoneal kidneys.

notes.A: The right lobe lies under the right dome of the diaphragm, with much of the liver deep to the lower right ribs.
notes.B: The fundus and upper body of the stomach lie beneath the left costal margin and left hemidiaphragm.
notes.C: The spleen typically lies deep to the ninth through eleventh left ribs, with its long axis near the tenth.
notes.D: The higher left kidney has posterior relations to the eleventh and twelfth ribs, with intervening diaphragm superiorly.
notes.E: The right kidney usually lies lower, but its upper posterior region still relates to the twelfth rib.

ana-ms15-45.why: The transpyloric plane is higher than the subcostal plane. It is conventionally near the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra, while the subcostal plane is nearer the third lumbar vertebra.

notes.A: The pylorus often lies on or near this plane in the supine individual, although its position changes with gastric filling.
notes.B: The gallbladder fundus usually lies near the right ninth costal cartilage at the level of the transpyloric plane.
notes.C: The ninth costal cartilage tips are landmarks where the transpyloric plane meets the costal margin.
notes.D: The conventional vertebral reference is the lower border of the first lumbar vertebral body.

ana-gpq-125.why: Two sagittal and two transverse planes divide the anterior abdomen into nine regions. The superior transverse plane may be subcostal or transpyloric, depending on the convention used, while the lower plane passes through the iliac tubercles.

notes.B: The transpyloric plane at approximately L1 can replace the subcostal plane as the upper transverse boundary.
notes.C: The intercristal plane joins the highest iliac crest points and is a different surface landmark from the intertubercular plane used in the grid.
notes.A: The subcostal plane is a common upper boundary and passes through the lowest points of the costal margins.
notes.D: The intertubercular plane passes through the iliac tubercles and separates the middle abdominal regions from the lower regions.
notes.E: Paired midclavicular planes form the vertical divisions and continue inferiorly towards the midinguinal points.

ana-gpq-126.why: Abdominal surface planes use palpable landmarks to describe the positions of deeper organs. The intertubercular and intercristal planes are transverse, while the paired midclavicular planes descend vertically.

notes.C: Both iliac tubercles are joined by the same horizontal plane, which is a transverse rather than vertical landmark.
notes.A: The midclavicular plane is conventionally extended to the point halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis.
notes.B: The transpyloric plane lies halfway between the jugular notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.
notes.D: The lowest points of the tenth costal cartilages define the subcostal plane near the third lumbar vertebra.
notes.E: The intercristal line joins the highest points of the iliac crests, near the fourth lumbar level.

ana-g16-a50.why: The conventional transverse thoracic plane extends from the sternal angle, where the second costal cartilages attach, to the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. It separates superior and inferior mediastinal regions.

notes.B: The lower border of T4 is adjacent to the T4–T5 disc, the posterior landmark of this division.

ana-mic-sa-e-46.why: Inguinal refers to the groin and lumbar refers here to the loin. The perineum is the pelvic outlet region around the external genitalia and anus, including the interval between them.

notes.B: The groin is inguinal. The loin is lumbar, rather than the second and third regions listed here.
notes.C: The first two labels are accurate, but the perineum includes both the anal and external genital regions.
notes.D: The loin correctly identifies the lumbar region, while the groin belongs first with the inguinal lesion.
notes.E: The inguinal region is specifically the groin, and the perineum includes the anal region as well as external genital structures.

ana-mic-sa-e-83.why: The ovaries produce oocytes and reproductive hormones. The uterine tubes transport gametes and support fertilisation and early cleavage, while the uterus provides the endometrium in which the blastocyst can implant.

notes.E: The kidneys filter blood and excrete nitrogenous wastes such as urea in the urine.
notes.A: Ovarian follicles contain developing oocytes and produce hormones that regulate the reproductive cycle.
notes.B: Fertilisation usually occurs in the uterine tube, whereas implantation occurs in the uterine endometrium.
notes.C: Tubal and uterine secretions support early development as the conceptus travels towards the implantation site.
notes.D: The tube provides a route for sperm to reach the oocyte and transports the oocyte or early embryo towards the uterus.

ana-mic-sa-e-84.why: Contraction of skeletal muscle produces force for movement, expression and posture. Muscle metabolism also releases heat, while the mineralised skeleton provides the major long-term calcium and phosphate store.

notes.E: Bone matrix stores calcium and phosphate in mineral crystals. Skeletal muscle is primarily a contractile tissue.
notes.A: Muscles acting across the upper-limb joints allow the hands to manipulate tools and other objects.
notes.B: Limb muscles move the body, while the muscles of facial expression pull on skin to change facial appearance.
notes.C: Sustained activity in postural muscles helps support body position against gravity even during quiet standing.
notes.D: Contraction releases heat as chemical energy is converted to work, and shivering increases heat production.

ana-mic-sa-e-118.why: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing, dysphonia means altered voice, and dyspnoea means difficult or uncomfortable breathing. Pharynx, larynx and lungs are the best corresponding sites among the choices, although the symptoms have wider causes.

notes.B: The larynx is central to phonation, so it corresponds to dysphonia, the second symptom in the sequence.
notes.C: The pharynx can be involved in swallowing difficulty, while a change in voice is more directly linked to the larynx.
notes.D: Middle ear dysfunction primarily affects hearing or pressure sensation. Dysphagia describes difficulty moving material from the mouth towards the stomach.
notes.E: The lungs can contribute to breathlessness, which is the last symptom. Dysphagia relates to the act of swallowing.

ana-mic-sa-g-65.why: Anatomical variation means a difference in physical form between individuals. A skin web between digits and a local area of differently pigmented hair are structural findings whose significance depends on clinical context.

notes.A: A difference in physical form alone does not establish a disease or indicate whether it has functional effects.
notes.B: Digit webbing may be congenital, but the examples give too little information to classify either finding as a serious defect.
notes.D: Tinnitus is a perception of sound, and albinism affects melanin production more broadly than an isolated white streak.
notes.E: Agenesis is failure of a structure to form. Both examples describe structures that are present with a difference in form or colour.

ana-mic-sa-g-66.why: Hepatitis is inflammation of liver tissue. Glomerulonephritis refers to inflammation involving renal glomeruli, the capillary structures that filter blood at the beginning of each nephron.

notes.A: The gallbladder stores bile and its inflammation is called cholecystitis, a different process from glomerulonephritis.
notes.B: The glomeruli are in the kidney and correspond to the second term, while hepatitis refers to the liver first.
notes.D: The liver is the organ affected in hepatitis, and the gallbladder lacks the glomerular structures named in the second term.
notes.E: Urinary bladder inflammation is cystitis, while gallbladder inflammation is cholecystitis.

ana-mic-sa-g-71.why: Oophorectomy is removal of an ovary, and hysterectomy is removal of the uterus. These are distinct operations because the ovaries may be retained when a hysterectomy is performed.

notes.A: The hymen is tissue at the vaginal opening and is anatomically separate from the uterus removed at hysterectomy.
notes.B: Removal of a uterine fibroid while retaining the uterus is called myomectomy.
notes.D: Removal of the uterus is hysterectomy, which is the second term. Oophorectomy refers to the ovary first.
notes.E: A hydatidiform mole is abnormal gestational tissue. Its removal is distinct from the definition of hysterectomy.

ana-mic-sa-g-72.why: Arthritis describes joint disease and includes inflammatory and degenerative forms. Gout reflects the inflammatory response to urate crystals, while other inflammation terms identify different organs by their anatomical roots.

notes.D: Orchitis is inflammation of the testis. Inflammation of the epididymis is termed epididymitis.
notes.E: Colitis is inflammation of the colon and has no anatomical connection to the cone cells of the retina.
notes.A: Arthritis covers a range of joint disorders that may feature synovial inflammation, articular degeneration or both.
notes.B: Osteoarthritis affects the whole joint, including progressive articular cartilage loss and changes in the underlying bone.
notes.C: Gout occurs when monosodium urate crystals accumulate in joint tissues and provoke an inflammatory response.
