ana-mic-sa-g-73.why: Cholecystitis refers to inflammation of the bile-storing gallbladder. In urinary clinical terminology, cystitis refers to inflammation of the urinary bladder, the reservoir for urine.

notes.A: The urinary bladder corresponds to cystitis, while inflammation of a uterine tube is termed salpingitis.
notes.B: The gallbladder matches the first term, while inflammation of the testis is called orchitis.
notes.D: The testis is affected in orchitis and the uterine tube in salpingitis. Both terms refer to reproductive organs.
notes.E: Inflammation of the liver is hepatitis. Cholecystitis specifically involves the gallbladder.

ana-mic-sa-g-105.why: The kidneys remove metabolic wastes and adjust the amount of water, electrolytes and acid excreted in urine. These processes help maintain the internal environment as intake and metabolism vary.

notes.E: The liver converts much of the nitrogen from amino acid metabolism into urea, which the kidneys then excrete.
notes.A: Urea and other nitrogenous wastes leave the bloodstream and are eliminated in the urine.
notes.B: The kidneys reabsorb and generate bicarbonate and excrete acid, helping regulate blood pH.
notes.C: The kidneys change urine volume and concentration to conserve water or remove a surplus.
notes.D: Tubular transport adjusts sodium, potassium and other electrolyte losses according to physiological demand.

ana-mic-sa-g-106.why: The cardiovascular system moves blood between lungs, digestive organs, tissues and excretory organs. It therefore transports useful materials to cells and carries wastes away for elimination or processing.

notes.C: Bile acts in the digestive tract and is produced by the liver. The circulation mainly transports materials between organs.
notes.D: Hepatocytes carry out the urea cycle, while blood carries the resulting urea to the kidneys.
notes.A: Blood carries oxygen from lungs to tissues and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs for exhalation.
notes.B: Circulation delivers absorbed nutrients to tissues and brings waste products to organs that process or excrete them.

ana-mic-sa-g-108.why: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system and integrate incoming information. Peripheral nerves and associated ganglia connect those central structures to receptors, muscles and glands.

notes.D: There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves and thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves in the conventional count.
notes.A: The standard anatomical division recognises central structures and peripheral nerves and ganglia linking them to the body.
notes.B: Cranial and spinal nerves account for much of the peripheral system, along with their branches and associated ganglia.
notes.C: The brain and spinal cord process signals and coordinate motor, autonomic and other responses.

ana-sa-d-83.why: Long bones store mineral in their matrix and contain marrow for blood cell formation or fat storage. In growing bones, cartilage at the epiphyseal plates also provides a template for longitudinal growth.

notes.A: Yellow marrow contains adipocytes that store lipid within the medullary cavities of many adult long bones.
notes.B: Thyroid hormones are secreted by follicular cells of the thyroid gland, outside the skeletal system.
notes.C: Chondrocytes proliferate and make cartilage at growth plates of immature long bones, before the tissue is replaced by bone.
notes.D: Red marrow produces blood cells, including at some proximal long-bone sites in adults.
notes.E: The mineralised matrix of long bones stores calcium and phosphate as part of the body's skeletal reserve.

ana-sa-d-89.why: A low-energy fracture and generalised thinning of bone suggest osteoporosis. Loss of bone quantity and architecture weakens the skeleton even when the remaining matrix is appropriately mineralised.

notes.A: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone and would require findings supporting infection in addition to fragility.
notes.B: Bone mass falls when resorption exceeds the formation of new bone over successive remodelling cycles.
notes.C: After menopause, reduced oestrogen can increase bone resorption and accelerate loss of bone mass.
notes.D: Defective mineralisation of bone matrix characterises osteomalacia, while osteoporosis reduces bone mass and disrupts architecture.
notes.E: Rickets involves impaired mineralisation at growing epiphyseal plates in children and does not explain this adult pattern.

ana-sa-d-92.why: Cartilage has a hydrated matrix that can deform under load and lacks its own blood vessels. Bone has a vascular, mineralised matrix, providing greater stiffness and generally faster repair than adult articular cartilage.

notes.A: Water bound within the cartilage matrix helps it regain shape after compression and distribute loads.
notes.B: Cartilage is particularly adapted to withstand compression, while marked shear can injure the tissue.
notes.C: Cartilage relies on diffusion for nutrition, but bone has vessels in its canals and marrow.
notes.D: Cartilage can expand through division of chondrocytes within its matrix, enabling rapid growth at developing skeletal sites.
notes.E: Adult cartilage has limited repair capacity because it lacks a direct vascular supply and contains relatively few cells.

ana-sa-e-2.why: Fontanelles are flexible connective tissue gaps between developing skull bones. They allow the head to mould during delivery and leave room for brain growth before the adult suture landmarks form.

notes.A: The diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle is usually closed by the end of the second year, with variation between infants.
notes.B: Open sutures and fontanelles allow skull expansion as the infant's brain increases in size.
notes.C: If a suture fuses early, skull growth is restricted in one direction and can produce an altered head shape.
notes.D: The flexible gaps allow the cranial bones to shift slightly relative to each other during birth.
notes.E: The anterior fontanelle marks the future bregma. Lambda marks the junction at the posterior fontanelle.

ana-sa-e-4.why: Typical cervical vertebrae have relatively large triangular vertebral foramina and transverse foramina. Their spinous processes project posteriorly, and the atlas, axis and seventh cervical vertebra have distinctive features.

notes.A: Typical bifid spinous processes project backwards from the vertebral arch, away from the body.
notes.B: A relatively broad triangular vertebral foramen accommodates the cervical spinal cord and its coverings.
notes.C: Each transverse process has a transverse foramen, although the structures passing through it vary with level.
notes.D: The seventh cervical vertebra usually has a long palpable spine and is conventionally called the vertebra prominens.
notes.E: The atlas and axis articulate through synovial joints and have no intervertebral disc between them.

ana-sa-e-6.why: Lumbar vertebrae support a substantial load through large bodies and intervertebral discs. Their processes lack the transverse foramina of the cervical region and the costal articular facets of the thoracic region.

notes.A: Lumbar discs transmit considerable load, and lower lumbar levels are common sites of disc herniation.
notes.B: Lumbar vertebral bodies are broad and roughly kidney shaped when viewed from above.
notes.C: Transverse foramina are cervical landmarks. Typical lumbar transverse processes have no such opening.
notes.D: Lumbar vertebrae lack the costal facets that allow thoracic vertebrae to articulate with the ribs.
notes.E: Costal facets on transverse processes represent a thoracic feature where the process articulates with a rib tubercle.

ana-sa-e-7.why: The first seven rib pairs reach the sternum through their own cartilages. Ribs eight through ten generally join the costal margin indirectly, and the two lowest pairs have no anterior sternal attachment.

notes.A: Seven pairs are vertebrosternal. The eighth joins the costal margin through another cartilage rather than reaching the sternum directly.
notes.B: The cartilages of ribs eight through ten join the cartilage above to help form the costal margin.
notes.C: Ribs eleven and twelve are short floating ribs with anterior ends that lack attachment to the sternum.
notes.D: Vertebrochondral ribs reach the sternum indirectly through other costal cartilage. The first seven have direct attachments.
notes.E: A typical rib has a head and neck near the vertebra, a tubercle, an angle and a curved shaft.

ana-sa-e-13.why: Side a scapula by facing its smooth concave surface towards the thorax and placing the spine posteriorly. The glenoid cavity then points laterally on the side to which the bone belongs.

notes.A: The subscapular fossa is the broad concavity on the anterior surface that rests against the rib cage.
notes.B: The posterior spine extends laterally to become the acromion, which overhangs the shoulder joint.
notes.C: The glenoid cavity faces laterally near the upper part of the bone, and the acromion projects above it.
notes.D: The spine divides the dorsal surface into a smaller supraspinous fossa and a larger infraspinous fossa.
notes.E: The costal surface contains the subscapular fossa. The fossae above and below the spine lie posteriorly.

ana-sa-e-14.why: The humeral head and tubercles form the proximal end at the shoulder. The shaft extends to the articular condyle and epicondyles distally, where the humerus meets the forearm bones.

notes.A: The humeral head articulates with the scapular glenoid cavity at the glenohumeral joint.
notes.B: The shaft unites the expanded proximal and distal ends and provides attachment surfaces for arm muscles.
notes.C: The capitulum, trochlea and flanking epicondyles are features of the distal end near the elbow.
notes.D: The anatomical neck surrounds the humeral head, and the greater and lesser tubercles lie nearby for tendon attachments.
notes.E: The distal end has epicondyles, whereas the greater and lesser tubercles are landmarks of the proximal end.

ana-sa-e-17.why: The femur is the major weight-bearing long bone of the thigh. Its proximal head articulates with the pelvis, and its distal condyles transmit forces to the tibia at the knee.

notes.A: The femur is normally the longest and heaviest bone in the human skeleton.
notes.B: Load passes from the acetabulum to the femoral head and shaft, then through the condyles to the tibia.
notes.C: The proximal femoral projections are the greater and lesser trochanters. The named greater and lesser tubercles belong to the humerus.
notes.D: The distal femur has two condyles and adjacent epicondyles. Its trochanters lie near the proximal neck.
notes.E: The femur has a long shaft and expanded ends, which place it in the long-bone category.

ana-sa-e-20.why: The skull includes broad plates protecting the brain and more complex bones forming the cranial base and face. Those shapes give common examples of flat and irregular bones.

notes.A: The sphenoid and ethmoid are irregular bones with complex contours around several cranial or facial spaces.
notes.B: The frontal and parietal bones form broad protective plates in the cranial vault and are classified as flat bones.
notes.C: Short bones are exemplified by carpals and most tarsals rather than the standard skull bones.
notes.D: Long bones have a shaft and two ends, a pattern characteristic of much of the appendicular skeleton.
notes.E: Sesamoid bones develop within tendons, as the patella does, and are not a standard skull bone category.

ana-sa-e-22.why: Irregular bones have complex shapes that do not fit the long, short or flat categories. Vertebrae and several bones of the cranial base and face are examples.

notes.A: Vertebrae have complex bodies and processes, while bones such as the sphenoid have similarly irregular outlines.
notes.B: The tibia and fibula are long bones, and most carpals of the wrist are short bones.
notes.C: The humerus is a long bone. Some skull bones are irregular, but the arm does not supply the matching example.
notes.D: Several skull bones are irregular, while the carpals are conventionally classified as short bones apart from special cases.
notes.E: The vertebral column contains irregular bones, but the standard shape category for most wrist bones is short.

ana-sa-e-23.why: Short bones have broadly similar length, width and thickness. Most carpals and tarsals are conventionally placed in this category, providing stability and limited movement in the wrist and foot.

notes.A: The framework of the leg between knee and ankle consists of tibia and fibula, both long bones.
notes.B: The humerus is the long bone of the anatomical arm between shoulder and elbow.
notes.C: Vertebrae are irregular bones because their processes and arches produce complex shapes.
notes.D: Most carpal bones are compact short bones forming the wrist at the proximal end of the hand.
notes.E: The tarsus contains several short bones, including the cuboid and cuneiforms, around the ankle and hindfoot.

ana-sa-e-25.why: At birth, several skeletal elements remain separate that later unite during growth. Fusion of parts of the skull, pelvis and vertebral column helps reduce the conventional count of separate bones by adulthood.

notes.A: Early in fetal development much of the skeleton is still cartilaginous and ossification centres have yet to appear.
notes.B: A newborn has multiple separate skeletal elements that later fuse, giving the highest conventional count among these choices.
notes.C: By ten years some elements, such as separate parts of the mandible, have already united.
notes.D: An adult skeleton usually has about 206 named bones after the normal developmental fusions.
notes.E: The higher conventional number of separate elements in the newborn provides a matching choice.

ana-sa-e-26.why: These labels distinguish different surface features. A foramen is a hole, a fissure a narrow slit, and a fossa a depression. An open channel is a groove, while a pneumatic sinus is a lined cavity.

notes.B: A sinus is a cavity within bone, while an elongated open channel on its surface is a groove.
notes.C: A fossa is a depression and a foramen passes through bone, so the first and third labels are reversed.
notes.D: A fissure describes a narrow slit. The wide depression in the sequence is a fossa.
notes.E: A complete hole through bone is a foramen, whereas a narrow cleft is called a fissure.

ana-sa-e-28.why: The two malleoli are the distal projections of the lower-leg bones that frame the ankle. The tibial projection is medial, while the fibular projection is lateral and usually extends farther down.

notes.A: Styloid names a slender pointed process elsewhere. The ankle projections of the distal tibia and fibula are the malleoli.
notes.B: The tibia lies medially and gives the medial malleolus. The fibula forms the lateral projection.
notes.D: Epicondyles are projections near a condyle. The bony sides of the ankle are named the malleoli.
notes.E: The fibular head and tibial tuberosity are proximal landmarks near the knee, far above the ankle.

ana-sa-e-29.why: The cuboid belongs to the tarsus on the lateral side of the foot. The trapezium and trapezoid are in the distal carpal row, while the triquetral and pisiform are on the ulnar side of the wrist.

notes.A: The trapezium is the distal carpal that articulates with the base of the first metacarpal.
notes.B: The trapezoid lies in the distal carpal row near the base of the second metacarpal.
notes.C: The triquetral is a bone in the proximal carpal row on the ulnar side of the wrist.
notes.D: The pisiform is a small sesamoid carpal within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.

ana-sa-e-32.why: The ischial tuberosities are the weight-bearing prominences of the pelvis in sitting. In the foot, the plantar surface of the calcaneus forms the bony support of the heel.

notes.A: The acetabulum is the hip socket, and the cuboid lies lateral and anterior to the principal heel bone.
notes.B: The calcaneus is the heel bone, but the iliac blade is the upper part of the hip bone rather than the sitting prominence.
notes.D: The ischium provides the sitting prominence, but the navicular lies in the medial midfoot.
notes.E: The talus receives load at the ankle, while the coccyx forms the terminal portion of the spine.

ana-sa-e-33.why: The greater and lesser tubercles lie near the humeral head and provide tendon attachment sites. Between them the intertubercular groove carries the tendon of the long head of biceps.

notes.A: The greater trochanter and intertrochanteric crest are proximal femoral landmarks. The lesser tubercle is on the humerus.
notes.B: Both tubercles belong to the proximal humerus, but the intercondylar fossa separates the distal femoral condyles.
notes.C: Both trochanters lie on the proximal femur, although the bicipital groove belongs to the humerus.
notes.D: Tuberosity can be used for the humeral tubercles, but the intertrochanteric crest joins the two femoral trochanters.

ana-sa-e-35.why: The thoracic and sacral curves retain the posterior convexity of the early spine. Cervical and lumbar curves develop in the opposite direction as the infant gains head control and adopts an upright posture.

notes.A: The thoracic and sacral curves are primary. The lumbar curve becomes distinct during later postural development.
notes.B: The thoracic and sacral segments are convex posteriorly, corresponding to the general curve present at birth.
notes.C: Cervical and lumbar curvatures are the secondary curves. The sacral curve is present earlier.
notes.D: Cervical and lumbar lordoses are convex anteriorly, opposite the thoracic and sacral kyphoses.
notes.E: Lumbar lordosis helps position trunk weight over the legs in standing. The sacral curve retains a primary posterior convexity.

ana-sa-e-39.why: The sternum forms the flat anterior midline plate of the thoracic cage. Its manubrium, body and xiphoid process provide attachments for costal cartilages, and the manubriosternal angle marks the second rib level.

notes.A: The xiphoid process ossifies relatively late, often around mid-adulthood, with substantial variation between individuals.
notes.C: Although it has three named subdivisions, the sternum is classified as a flat bone.
notes.D: The second costal cartilage joins the sternum at its angle, allowing other rib levels to be counted from it.
notes.E: Each of the first seven ribs has a costal cartilage that reaches the sternum directly.
notes.B: The sternum lies anterior to the mediastinum and protects the underlying heart and nearby structures.

ana-sa-e-40.why: Humans usually have twelve rib pairs. The first seven attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages. The remaining pairs attach indirectly or, for the last two, end without an anterior attachment.

notes.A: The usual total is twelve pairs, corresponding to the twelve levels of the thoracic vertebral column.
notes.B: Ribs one to seven are true ribs because their cartilages connect them directly to the sternum.
notes.C: The eighth pair also lacks an independent sternal attachment, so the non-true group starts at rib eight.
notes.D: Ribs eleven and twelve are floating. The tenth generally joins the costal margin through its cartilage.
notes.E: The last two ribs terminate anteriorly without attaching to the sternum or another costal cartilage.

ana-sa-e-41.why: The foramen magnum is the large skull-base opening connecting the cranial cavity with the vertebral canal. It lies within the occipital bone, which meets the parietals posteriorly at the lambdoid suture.

notes.A: The foramen magnum permits continuity of the lower brainstem and spinal cord across the skull base.
notes.B: The basilar, lateral and squamous parts of the occipital bone enclose the foramen magnum.
notes.C: The lambdoid suture joins the occipital and parietal bones. The sagittal suture runs between the two parietals.
notes.D: The lambdoid suture lies posteriorly and separates the parietal bones from the occipital bone.
notes.E: The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the parietals, which meet each other at the sagittal suture.

ana-sa-e-43.why: Typical lumbar vertebrae have large bodies for load bearing and short, thick spinous processes. Their transverse processes extend laterally and lack the foramina or rib facets characteristic of other regions.

notes.A: The broad kidney-shaped lumbar body provides a substantial surface for transferring load to the disc below.
notes.B: The lumbar transverse processes are conspicuous lateral projections, with their length varying by vertebral level.
notes.C: Transverse foramina perforate cervical transverse processes. The corresponding lumbar processes are solid.
notes.D: A typical lumbar spinous process is thick, blunt and directed posteriorly rather than markedly inferiorly.
notes.E: Lumbar vertebrae lack the costal articular facets involved in the rib articulations of the thoracic region.

ana-sa-e-119.why: The clavicle is an S-shaped long bone spanning the upper thorax. Its bulky medial end joins the sternum, while its flattened lateral end joins the acromion and helps hold the shoulder laterally.

notes.C: Its strut function keeps the scapula and arm lateral to the chest and transmits upper-limb forces medially.
notes.D: The medial sternal end is relatively bulky. The lateral acromial end is the flattened end.
notes.E: The lateral end articulates with the acromion, while the rounded medial end articulates with the manubrium.
notes.A: The clavicle is a curved long bone with a shaft linking a sternal end to an acromial end.
notes.B: The collarbone has a roughly horizontal course between the superior sternum and shoulder tip.

ana-sa-g-17.why: The hip bone forms from the fused ilium, ischium and pubis around the acetabulum. It joins the sacrum behind and the opposite pubis in front to help complete the pelvic ring.

notes.A: The ilium articulates with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint to transmit load between trunk and lower limbs.
notes.B: The three components join around the acetabulum, whose developmental cartilage later ossifies.
notes.E: The pubic symphysis contains a fibrocartilaginous disc between articular surfaces, rather than elastic cartilage.
notes.C: The two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx together form the bony pelvis.
notes.D: The hip bone is irregular and its acetabulum receives the head of the femur.

ana-sa-g-18.why: The two hip bones join the sacrum and coccyx to form the bony pelvis. Its inlet and outlet bound the lesser pelvis, and their proportions are clinically important in childbirth.

notes.A: The hip bones form the lateral walls, while the sacrum and coccyx complete the posterior part of the bony pelvis.
notes.B: On average the female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a wider subpubic angle that accommodates childbirth.
notes.C: The inlet lies at the pelvic brim. The outlet is the lower opening of the bony pelvis.
notes.D: The pubic arch, ischial tuberosities and coccyx are anterior, lateral and posterior landmarks of the outlet respectively.
notes.E: Pelvic features such as the subpubic angle and sciatic notch help estimate skeletal sex, with individual overlap.

ana-sa-g-36.why: The coronal suture extends across the skull vault and joins the frontal bone to the paired parietal bones. It forms the anterior boundary of the parietal region on each side.

notes.B: The squamous suture joins the temporal squama to the adjacent parietal bone on the lateral skull.
notes.C: The temporal bones lie on opposite sides of the skull and do not meet each other at a midline suture.
notes.D: The parietal bones meet in the midline at the sagittal suture, which runs backwards from the coronal suture.
notes.E: The occipitomastoid suture is the junction between the temporal and occipital bones near the skull base.

ana-sa-g-61.why: The sternum consists of a manubrium superiorly, an elongated body in the middle and a xiphoid process inferiorly. The second costal cartilage marks the junction between the manubrium and body.

notes.B: The xiphoid and body belong to the sternum. Intervertebral discs lie between vertebral bodies in the spine.
notes.C: Costal cartilage connects ribs to the sternum, while the malleus is an auditory ossicle in the middle ear.
notes.D: The manubrium belongs to the sternum, but the incus is a middle-ear bone and elastic cartilage is a tissue.
notes.E: The xiphoid and manubrium are sternal parts. The vomer helps form the bony nasal septum.

ana-sa-g-62.why: The patella lies in the quadriceps tendon at the front of the knee and is the largest sesamoid bone. The palatine and occipital bones in its group both belong to the skull.

notes.A: The parietal forms part of the vault, while the ethmoid and vomer contribute to the nasal region of the skull.
notes.B: The frontal and temporal bones contribute to the cranium, and the maxilla forms much of the upper jaw.
notes.C: The nasal, zygomatic and lacrimal bones are facial bones contributing to the nose, cheek or medial orbital wall.
notes.E: The mandible forms the lower jaw, and the malleus and incus are small bones of the middle ear.
